definition: The end-state of the Hook model where the product attaches itself to a pre-existing emotion (boredom, loneliness, anxiety) so the user opens it automatically with no external prompt.
why_it_works: After enough repetition a negative emotional state becomes a trigger the user resolves by reflexively opening the app — the deepest most durable engagement, needing no notification.
product_examples: The reflexive phone-check at any idle moment; opening Instagram/TikTok/X without deciding to
how_to_apply: Building habits is legitimate for genuinely valuable products; the ethical fork (Eyal's manipulation matrix) is whether the habit improves the user's life.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: dark when the habit serves the platform at the user's expense

definition: A machine-learning feed that ranks and serves content predicted to maximize engagement, learned continuously from watch time, replays, likes and dwell.
why_it_works: Delivers a variable reward of near-perfect novelty — the algorithm gets better at predicting the next thing you can't look away from, delivering a high-reward hit every few clips in an intermittent schedule.
product_examples: TikTok For You; Instagram Reels/Explore; YouTube recommendations & Shorts; X For You
how_to_apply: Optimize for stated user satisfaction over raw watch time, expose why-am-I-seeing-this, offer a chronological option, and inject diversity.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: optimizing purely for engagement vs user-stated value maximizes consumption against reflective interest

definition: Use onboarding inputs (goals, current habits, schedule, energy) and ongoing behavior to generate a plan tailored to the individual.
why_it_works: Relevance raises perceived value and self-efficacy; tailored plans fit the user's real life, reducing friction and the this-isn't-for-me dropout — the secret sauce of sticky wellness programs.
product_examples: Noom's personalized program from intake; Zero Fast's ML weekly plans; meditation apps recommending by goal
how_to_apply: Collect just enough at onboarding (~2 min) to personalize then keep adapting from behavior; recommend, don't overwhelm.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Ask a few targeted questions then immediately customize the first experience (content, templates, goals) to the answers.
why_it_works: A short personalization quiz raised Headspace course starts +7.6 pts; relevance shortens time-to-value and the act of asking signals listening (IKEA/feeling-seen), making the experience feel like mine.
product_examples: Spotify artist/genre picker; Headspace path self-selection; TikTok interest-inferring first feed; Duolingo goal/level questions
how_to_apply: Ask the minimum questions that materially change the first experience, show value immediately after, and never collect data you won't use.
dark_pattern: No: unless the survey is a pretext to harvest data without delivering tailored value

definition: Dynamically adjusting task difficulty to the learner's current ability to keep them in the flow channel.
why_it_works: Keeps users in flow — the channel between boredom and anxiety — by calibrating difficulty to keep success rates in the productive ~80% zone; sustained flow is highly engaging.
product_examples: Brain-training apps (Peak, Elevate, Lumosity adaptive levels); Duolingo personalized practice; Memrise adaptive review
how_to_apply: Continuously calibrate difficulty to keep success rates in the productive zone.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Dashboards, graphs and trend views that turn invisible effort into visible progress — total minutes, sessions, streaks, mood over time.
why_it_works: The progress principle (Amabile) — visible progress is one of the strongest daily motivators; visualization makes intangible wellness work tangible and proves the behavior counts.
product_examples: Headspace/Calm total-minutes dashboards; Zero's trend views; Daylio's mood-vs-activity charts
how_to_apply: Show cumulative and trend data prominently, make progress legible at a glance, and celebrate milestones inside it.
dark_pattern: No: obsessive metric-watching can backfire; offer the ability to dial it down

definition: Translate sensor data (sleep, HRV, resting HR) into plain-English daily guidance — a readiness/recovery/sleep score telling you what today calls for.
why_it_works: Self-perception and feedback theory — concrete personalized data makes cause-and-effect visible (I slept badly because I drank late), creating a learning loop that motivates change better than generic advice.
product_examples: Oura's three morning scores; Whoop's strain/recovery coach; Sleep Cycle's analysis
how_to_apply: Don't just show numbers — interpret them into a single actionable verdict and tie it to the user's controllable behaviors.
dark_pattern: No: score anxiety (orthosomnia) is a risk; frame scores as guidance not judgment

definition: Quick logging of mood and contextual factors that over time surfaces patterns (your mood dips on low-sleep days).
why_it_works: Self-monitoring is itself an evidence-based behavior-change technique (the reactivity effect) and correlation views validate hunches and build self-knowledge.
product_examples: Daylio's two-tap mood+activity with correlation stats; Stoic's reflection; Finch's daily mood check-ins
how_to_apply: Make logging near-frictionless (taps not typing) and close the loop by showing the user what their data reveals; logging with insight is a reward.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Structured prompts (morning intention, evening review, gratitude, reframing) that turn writing into a recurring practice with a skill being built.
why_it_works: Expressive writing and structured reflection improve wellbeing; Stoicism is the intellectual ancestor of CBT so its prompts do real cognitive reframing, and repeating a structure builds a skill.
product_examples: Stoic's morning prep / evening review; gratitude apps; Finch's reflection prompts; Day One
how_to_apply: Provide scaffolded prompts rather than a blank page, anchor reflection to morning/evening rituals, and keep entries optionally short.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Deliver bite-size lessons explaining the science behind each suggested behavior, often grounded in CBT.
why_it_works: Understanding why increases buy-in and self-efficacy (Bandura) and CBT-based reframing changes the thoughts that drive behavior, converting blind compliance into informed durable motivation.
product_examples: Noom's daily psychology/CBT lessons; Fabulous explaining the science; Headspace's how-meditation-works explainers
how_to_apply: Attach a short plain-language rationale to each new habit — teach the principle then prescribe the action.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Sequence the experience as a themed multi-day journey, course or program with a beginning, middle and arc — not an open-ended pile of content.
why_it_works: A defined path reduces decision fatigue, creates a goal gradient (you can see the finish), and supplies narrative momentum, with each day unlocking the next (Zeigarnik).
product_examples: Headspace foundational courses; Calm's multi-day series; Fabulous's journeys layering habits gradually
how_to_apply: Package habits/sessions into named multi-day journeys with visible progress bars and a sense of arc, unlocking content sequentially.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Make the decision for the user when you can predict it well — auto-curate, auto-recommend, surprise-me or smart defaults — so they consume rather than choose.
why_it_works: Decision fatigue accumulates across a session, each choice depleting capacity; auto-picks remove the choosing entirely and prevent defaulting to nothing.
product_examples: Spotify Discover Weekly/Daylist; Netflix Play-something; TikTok algorithmic feed; Amazon Subscribe-and-Save
how_to_apply: Offer a strong default/auto-pick alongside manual choice, use behavior to curate, and provide a just-pick-for-me button.
dark_pattern: No: auto-feeds optimized purely for time-on-app shade into engagement traps

definition: Most active users use the product free; monetization (subscriptions, ads) layers on top of an engagement engine rather than gating the core.
why_it_works: Maximizes top-of-funnel and word-of-mouth; a tiny conversion of a massive engaged base outperforms paywalled rivals (Duolingo out-earns other education apps despite ~97% free usage).
product_examples: Duolingo Super/Max; Spotify free tier; most successful consumer apps
how_to_apply: Optimize engagement and reach first then monetize a small willing slice without degrading the free core.
dark_pattern: No

definition: Continuous large-scale experimentation (test-it-first) — thousands of A/B tests with hundreds running simultaneously — tuning every mechanic against retention.
why_it_works: Not a user-facing mechanic but the meta-engine: every pillar is tuned empirically, and sensitivity analysis reveals which knobs actually move DAU.
product_examples: Duolingo experiment platform; Booking.com, Netflix experimentation cultures
how_to_apply: Treat engagement as an empirical discipline, instrument everything, and let controlled experiments pick winners.
dark_pattern: No: amplifies whatever it optimizes for, so the chosen metric matters ethically

definition: A feed that loads new content continuously as the user scrolls, never reaching a bottom or natural end point.
why_it_works: Removes the stopping cue — the friction moment where a user would decide whether to continue — and exploits the Zeigarnik open loop the feed never closes; the structural backbone of feed addiction.
product_examples: TikTok For You; Instagram feed and Reels; X timeline; Facebook News Feed; Reddit
how_to_apply: Add deliberate stopping cues — you're-all-caught-up markers, pagination, session summaries, a natural end to a session's content.
dark_pattern: Yes: deliberately removes natural decision points to extend sessions, costing agency over time

definition: The gesture of dragging a feed downward to load new content, where the user does not know what (if anything) new will appear.
why_it_works: An intermittent variable reward (Skinner's variable-ratio) — the same structure that makes slot machines compulsive; unpredictability of the payout maximizes the dopamine of anticipation (the slot machine in your pocket).
product_examples: Email apps; X; Instagram; any feed with a pull gesture mimicking pulling a lever
how_to_apply: A refresh control can load new items predictably and quietly; the ethical version makes refreshing optional, transparent and not the primary path to content.
dark_pattern: Yes: repackages a utility as a gamble to exploit variable-reward conditioning

definition: Automatically playing the next video/episode (or scrolling to the next clip) with no user action required.
why_it_works: Eliminates the active decision to continue so the default becomes keep-watching; a Netflix study found disabling autoplay significantly reduced watching, and it ices over stopping cues, deepening the machine zone.
product_examples: YouTube autoplay + Shorts auto-advance; Netflix next episode; TikTok/Reels auto-loop; slot autoplay
how_to_apply: Make continue an explicit choice or at minimum an easy off switch and an are-you-still-watching check that genuinely pauses.
dark_pattern: Yes: removes the user's stop-and-reconsider decision to prolong sessions

definition: A trance-like state of calm equilibrium where time, money, social demands and the self dissolve, and the player plays not to win but to stay in the zone.
why_it_works: Schull's ethnography frames addiction as co-production of human and machine — the machine engineered for continuous productivity while the user seeks a self-liquidating state; smooth uninterrupted play sustains the zone.
product_examples: Video poker / continuous slot play; the doomscroll trance; binge-watching; all-night gaming
how_to_apply: Flow serves a goal the user endorses; the machine zone is flow without a goal — provide exits, stopping cues and are-you-still-there checks rather than removing them.
dark_pattern: Yes: the zone is the explicit design target, with harm following frictionless infinity

definition: A spin returns less than was wagered (a net loss) but is celebrated with the full winning fanfare (bet 75c, win 30c, but the machine throws a party).
why_it_works: LDWs trigger the same physiological arousal as real wins and cause players to dramatically overestimate how often they win; misremembered winning sustains play.
product_examples: Multiline slots; achievement-unlocked for trivial forced actions; You-saved-$X on a transaction that still cost money
how_to_apply: Celebrate genuine net-positive outcomes; never fire victory feedback on an outcome where the user is on net worse off.
dark_pattern: Yes: literally lying to the user's reward system about whether they won

definition: Wrapping every salient event — and many non-events — in synchronized lights, animations, music and haptics tuned to maximize arousal rather than clarity.
why_it_works: Positive sound reinforcement releases dopamine and makes players overestimate win frequency; audio/visual feedback anchors the behavior as positive and strengthens the conditioned response.
product_examples: Reel-stop jingles, jackpot sirens, coin-cascade sounds; ka-ching sale sounds attached to losses; gacha light-shows
how_to_apply: Sensory feedback is good UX when it confirms a real valued state change; attaching celebratory feedback to losses or tuning it to maximize arousal crosses into manipulation.
dark_pattern: Yes (as deployed in gambling): feedback calibrated to addict, not inform

pillar_name: Rapid Play Rate & Ultra-Short Feedback Loops
definition: Compressing the bet-outcome-bet cycle to a few seconds (modern slots run ~600 spins/hour) to outrun deliberation.
why_it_works: High event frequency is one of the strongest structural predictors of gambling harm — faster play impairs response inhibition, encourages larger wagers and accelerates losses before they register.
product_examples: Turbo spin, quick-bet; infinite scroll; autoplaying short-form video; one-tap reorder
how_to_apply: Speed is good for productive tasks; deliberately removing natural pauses from a consumption/spending loop to defeat reflective stopping is the harm — add friction before consequential actions.
dark_pattern: Yes: speed weaponized specifically to outrun deliberation

definition: Giving the player meaningless choices and inputs (a stop button, choosing your machine, nudging a reel) that feel like skill but cannot change a predetermined outcome.
why_it_works: People who choose feel they have better odds (Langer); skill-attribution after wins increases bet sizes, session length and chasing despite the result being fixed at spin start.
product_examples: Slot stop buttons; pick-your-bonus reveals (all pre-set); fake your-choices-shape-the-story branching that converges
how_to_apply: Real agency (choices that actually change outcomes) is honest; presenting fake agency over a fixed/random result to induce skill-illusion is the dark pattern.
dark_pattern: Yes: manufactures a false belief in skill to extend play

definition: Behaviors learned under intermittent reward persist far longer through dry spells than those learned under continuous reward, so gamblers keep going through losing streaks.
why_it_works: Because reward was always unpredictable, the absence of reward is indistinguishable from a normal gap — there's no clear signal it has stopped paying, so disengagement becomes irrationally hard.
product_examples: Continued play after dozens of losses; checking a now-boring feed because it used to be rewarding; persisting through unlucky gacha pulls
how_to_apply: Less a feature to apply than a consequence to be aware of — building intermittent reward also builds stubborn persistence after the product stops serving the user.
dark_pattern: Yes (as exploited): it is why losing players don't quit

definition: Purchasable randomized containers (loot boxes/gacha pulls) whose contents are unknown until opened, with rare valuable outcomes at low probability — structurally a slot pull.
why_it_works: Same variable-ratio plus near-miss plus suspense-reveal stack as slots; loot-box spending correlates with problem gambling, disproportionately affecting adolescents; Belgium and the Netherlands ruled certain forms gambling.
product_examples: Overwatch/CS loot crates; FIFA Ultimate Team packs; Genshin gacha; mystery boxes; digital blind boxes
how_to_apply: Randomized rewards can be acceptable only if odds are disclosed, spend is capped, no real money is required and items are cosmetic; paid randomized reward accessible to minors is gambling-by-another-name.
dark_pattern: Yes: gambling mechanics monetized; the debate is labeling not whether the psychology is the same

definition: A pity counter guarantees a rare item after N pulls, combined with limited-time banners featuring exclusive characters and a lose-the-50/50 mechanic.
why_it_works: Pity converts the gamble into a sunk-cost commitment device (once you've sunk 60 pulls quitting before 90 forfeits guaranteed value), and limited banners weaponize FOMO and time-scarcity.
product_examples: Genshin Impact; Honkai/Star Rail; Zenless Zone Zero; limited-edition countdown-gated cosmetics
how_to_apply: A guaranteed-after-N pity is more humane than pure randomness; it becomes predatory paired with manufactured scarcity and sunk-cost framing that pressures spend to not-waste pulls.
dark_pattern: Yes: engineered sunk-cost plus scarcity binding around random monetization

definition: Randomized physical or in-app rewards where you don't know what you'll get until after you commit — the surprise reveal is the product.
why_it_works: Variable reinforcement plus the anticipate-purchase-open-evaluate-repeat loop plus completion bias and FOMO over rarity tiers produces near-gambling engagement, exploiting kids' underdeveloped impulse control.
product_examples: Kinder Surprise, LOL Surprise, gashapon, Labubu blind boxes; gacha mobile games; foil card packs
how_to_apply: Use the anticipation-and-reveal feeling without the gambling spine — surprise-but-guaranteed rewards, transparent odds, no real-money randomization, daily free reveals.
dark_pattern: Yes: real-money randomized rewards marketed to children operate akin to gambling

definition: A depletable resource consumed by play that regenerates over time or via payment, capping how much a user can play per session.
why_it_works: Manufactures scarcity and a return-appointment; the cap creates a paywall (refill for 99c) and a stopping point that induces FOMO, monetizing impatience.
product_examples: Candy Crush lives; Duolingo hearts; most match-3/idle mobile titles
how_to_apply: Soft pacing can prevent binge-burnout, but the dominant intent is monetizing impatience; if you must pace do it transparently and don't sell the only escape.
dark_pattern: Yes: pay-to-skip-the-wait, artificially blocking willing play to sell skips

pillar_name: Hearts / Lives & the Cost of Mistakes
definition: Start with limited hearts, each wrong answer costs one, and at zero you wait, practice to refill, spend currency or subscribe to continue.
why_it_works: Loss aversion plus manufactured scarcity plus artificial waiting create urgency and a conversion lever; removing the limit is a core subscription selling point, so the friction exists partly to sell its own removal.
product_examples: Duolingo hearts (Super removes the limit); mobile-game lives/energy (Candy Crush)
how_to_apply: A small cost to mistakes can make accuracy feel consequential — but be cautious in a learning context where mistakes are the point of practice.
dark_pattern: Yes: monetization-of-frustration, pedagogically perverse for learning

definition: Convert real money into chips/coins/gems via a (often dual) currency system so the user never directly experiences spending dollars.
why_it_works: The double-currency model obfuscates real spend; virtual currency has no fixed real-world meaning, creating psychological distance that reduces the pain of paying, and awkward bundle sizes leave leftover balances prompting more buys.
product_examples: Casino chips; V-Bucks; Robux; Genesis Crystals to Primogems; arcade tickets
how_to_apply: Currencies are reasonable for closed economies with clear conversion; deliberately obscuring the real-money cost (odd denominations, multi-currency confusion) is the dark pattern.
dark_pattern: Yes: obfuscation exists to make people spend more than they realize

definition: Structuring economies so a small fraction of high-spending whales generate most revenue, with desirable content released on a cadence that pressures immediate purchase.
why_it_works: Most revenue concentrates in few users; emotional attachment, status and time-pressure drive disproportionate spend, and the whale-property all-in incentive emerges when the reward is deeply wanted.
product_examples: Genshin Impact; Clash of Clans; mobile RPGs broadly
how_to_apply: Understand the model exists; building it is an ethical choice — add spend caps, spending dashboards and parental controls if you monetize this way.
dark_pattern: Yes: deliberately engineering high spend in a vulnerable minority

definition: Selling the premium tier largely as removing self-imposed friction the product deliberately created — unlimited hearts, no ads, no waits.
why_it_works: The product deliberately creates frustrations whose removal is the value proposition; pain relief is an easier sell than added value.
product_examples: Duolingo Super (unlimited hearts); freemium games selling out of energy/wait timers
how_to_apply: A premium tier can sell no-more-annoyance, but design ethically so the base experience is still genuinely good.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: dark when the friction is engineered primarily so users pay to remove it

definition: Continuing and escalating wagering after losses to win it back, induced by perfectly-timed re-hooks.
why_it_works: Sunk-cost plus loss aversion plus gambler's fallacy; games are designed to induce this with near-miss teases, you-almost-won messages and bonuses that appear right after a bad run.
product_examples: Doubling-down after a losing streak; win-back offers after churn signals; discounts that appear when you're about to quit
how_to_apply: There is no good consumer version of engineering loss-chasing; ethical design interrupts it with limits and take-a-breather prompts.
dark_pattern: Yes: the exploitation lies in timing offers to the user's most vulnerable moment

definition: Encouraging false beliefs that an outcome is due after a streak (gambler's fallacy) or that a winning streak will continue (hot-hand) to sustain play.
why_it_works: Humans misperceive independent random events as self-correcting or momentum-carrying; both distortions correlate with problem gambling and big wins trigger fresh ones (I'm hot now).
product_examples: I'm-due-for-a-jackpot persistence; you're-on-a-roll momentum framing; streak/momentum UI implying non-existent trends
how_to_apply: Mostly a bias to protect users from; ethical design avoids copy/visuals encouraging false momentum or being-due beliefs.
dark_pattern: Yes (when exploited): fueling false momentum/due beliefs to sustain wagering

definition: Explicit on-screen messaging that frames a loss as a near-victory — So close!, You almost had it!, Just one more symbol!
why_it_works: The verbal/UI complement to the structural near-miss — it directs attention to how close the loss was, amplifying win-circuitry recruitment and try-again motivation, converting a loss into a near-success story.
product_examples: Slot almost overlays; gacha you-were-1-away; You-were-SO-close-to-your-goal; quiz Aww-almost screens
how_to_apply: Encouraging you're-nearly-there toward a real achievable goal is fine; framing a random or fixed loss as an almost-win to manufacture try-again arousal is exploitation.
dark_pattern: Yes (over random/non-skill outcomes): manufactured near-victory

pillar_name: Scratchcards / Daily-Spin Wheels (Gambling Skin on Apps)
definition: Pay or open a card/wheel/box for an instant-reveal random reward, often once per day, to drive habitual app opens.
why_it_works: Short payout schedule plus rapid event frequency plus instant gratification plus near-misses replicate slots; a reward that's won feels more valuable than the same reward shown plainly, and the daily cadence builds a habitual check-in.
product_examples: Lottery scratch-offs; e-commerce spin-to-win popups; fintech daily-spin; scratch-for-a-deal in food delivery
how_to_apply: A genuine daily bonus giving real unconditional value not tied to spending can be a fine delight; rigged-toward-discounts wheels that manufacture a daily compulsion loop are a gambling skin on a retention funnel.
dark_pattern: Yes (often): imports slot-machine variable reward into ordinary apps to drive compulsive opens

pillar_name: Social Casino Apps (Gambling Mechanics, No Payout)
definition: Free-to-play apps replicating slot/poker mechanics with no monetary payout, monetizing instead via in-app purchases of more chips/spins.
why_it_works: Strips gambling to its pure compulsion engine (variable ratio, near-miss, LDWs, sensory reinforcement) without the gambling regulatory burden; players pay real money for virtual chips that buy only more play.
product_examples: Slotomania; Big Fish Casino; House of Fun; Coin Master; Monopoly GO!
how_to_apply: If a game sells currency whose only use is to feed a variable-ratio loop with no out, it's compulsion-for-rent; ethical games sell durable value not refills for a Skinner box.
dark_pattern: Yes: arguably the purest commercialized compulsion engine, dodging gambling law via no-payout

pillar_name: Multiline Betting / Constant Reinforcement (Always Something Green)
definition: Structuring the experience so almost every interaction lights up a win — usually a partial win that nets a loss — manufacturing constant reinforcement to mask net loss or lack of progress.
why_it_works: More lines means more frequent wins lighting up, more near-misses and more arousal despite steady losses; multi-metric framing where something is always green masks a mostly-incomplete reality.
product_examples: Modern multiline video slots; dashboards with many tiny win/streak indicators all firing; you-completed-4-of-7-goals on a mostly-incomplete day
how_to_apply: Showing multiple progress signals is fine when they reflect reality; structuring it so almost every interaction lights up a win to mask net loss is the trap.
dark_pattern: Yes: multiline structure exists largely to multiply LDWs and near-misses

definition: Letting and encouraging players to raise bet-per-line, number of lines and machine denomination, escalating the amount at risk per spin.
why_it_works: Bigger bets raise win/LDW magnitudes and arousal, feed illusion-of-control (max-bet-to-win-the-jackpot) and accelerate the loss rate; skill-illusion after wins specifically increases bet sizes.
product_examples: Max-bet buttons; bet multipliers; high-limit rooms; upsell ladders; double-or-nothing offers
how_to_apply: Variable pricing is normal commerce; nudging users to escalate the amount at risk via skill-illusion and bigger-is-better-odds framing is exploitative — default to safe stakes.
dark_pattern: Yes: escalation framing pushes users to lose faster under an illusion of advantage

definition: A withdrawal pending period during which the player is nudged to reverse the withdrawal and gamble it back, plus wagering requirements and max-cashout caps that keep winnings trapped.
why_it_works: Exploits the asymmetry between fast deposits and slow reversible withdrawals, keeping money available to lose during a vulnerable window and leveraging chasing/impulse.
product_examples: Online casino reverse-withdrawal, bonus wagering requirements, withdrawal caps; cancel-flows that keep pausing instead of ending
how_to_apply: Withdrawals and cancellations should be at least as easy as deposits/sign-ups (symmetry of friction); any asymmetry making exit harder than entry is a roach motel.
dark_pattern: Yes: deliberately making cash-out/exit harder and reversible to recapture funds

pillar_name: Friction Asymmetry: Easy In, Hard Out (Roach Motel / Forced Continuity)
definition: Deliberately making starting/subscribing/buying frictionless while making leaving/canceling/refunding maximally difficult — the asymmetry is the manipulation.
why_it_works: Exploits inertia, status-quo bias and effort-aversion weaponized; roach motel hides cancellation (call-to-cancel, buried settings) and forced continuity silently converts a trial into recurring charges, so users stay because leaving costs too much effort.
product_examples: Gyms requiring in-person cancellation; call-us-to-cancel subscriptions; trials that auto-bill with no reminder
how_to_apply: Make canceling as easy as subscribing (FTC click-to-cancel), send pre-billing reminders, offer pause, and treat symmetric friction as the ethical test.
dark_pattern: Yes: the canonical dark pattern (roach motel + forced continuity)

definition: Friction-removal techniques inverted to manipulate: confirmshaming (guilt-wording the decline), sneaking pre-checked add-ons into the cart, and one-tap flows engineered to make spending/consent happen before reflection.
why_it_works: Borrows the same low-effort defaults, single-action design and persuasive copy that aid users but aims them at the company's goal — pre-checked boxes, shame-worded opt-outs and frictionless purchase remove the deliberation that would protect the user.
product_examples: No-thanks-I-like-paying-full-price decline links; pre-ticked insurance/marketing-consent boxes; sneak-into-basket add-ons
how_to_apply: Word decline options neutrally, never pre-check choices that cost the user money or privacy, and add a deliberate confirmation step for spending.
dark_pattern: Yes: catalogued deceptive patterns (confirmshaming, sneaking, forced-action)

definition: Accounts and content set to public/discoverable by default, requiring users to actively opt into privacy, with controls buried in privacy mazes.
why_it_works: Default bias — most users never change defaults, so default-public maximizes content supply, discoverability and growth; obstruction (9+ clicks, small text) makes privacy hard to find.
product_examples: Instagram public default; advertiser data-sharing defaults; Meta's documented obstructive opt-out process
how_to_apply: Default to the more private setting (privacy-by-default as GDPR requires), make controls easy to find, and present choices neutrally.
dark_pattern: Yes: default-public and buried controls are documented privacy dark patterns

pillar_name: Absence of Validation as Social Pain
definition: The negative emotional consequence when expected likes/comments don't arrive, which itself drives more checking and re-posting.
why_it_works: The absence of expected validation activates the same regions that process physical pain and social exclusion; the brain treats few-likes like being left out, making the like-economy a two-sided trap.
product_examples: Any platform with public engagement counts; the post-and-refresh-anxiously loop on Instagram and X
how_to_apply: Reduce the salience/publicness of counts; avoid designs where low engagement is broadcast as a visible failure.
dark_pattern: Yes: a system whose absence of reward inflicts measurable social pain that re-drives engagement

sub_category: social reward / variable reward of the tribe
definition: Quantified public positive feedback (likes, hearts, view counts) delivered unpredictably over time, layering slot-machine reinforcement on top of social reward.
why_it_works: Positive social feedback activates the same reward center as food/money/drugs, adolescents show heightened striatal activation, and variable timing makes validation a slot machine for self-worth.
product_examples: Instagram hearts; Facebook reactions; TikTok likes & view counts; X likes/reposts; YouTube thumbs-up
how_to_apply: If you use approval signals consider de-emphasizing public counts, hiding them by default, or making feedback qualitative rather than a leaderboard.
dark_pattern: Yes (as deployed): quantified variably-timed validation engineered into a self-esteem dependency, with documented teen harm

definition: Indicators showing a message has been read (Seen, Read, Delivered), creating an expectation of timely reply.
why_it_works: Read receipts convert ambiguity into a charged signal (they've seen it and chosen not to reply), invoking the reciprocity norm; ~93% admit to avoiding opening messages to dodge the read marker.
product_examples: Snapchat opened indicators; Instagram DMs; WhatsApp blue ticks; iMessage read receipts; Messenger Seen
how_to_apply: Make read receipts opt-in and symmetric and never tie them to obligation; recognize they raise engagement at the cost of anxiety.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: read receipts increase reply pressure and exploit reciprocity norms

definition: Content carrying high moral-emotional arousal (anger, outrage) that the algorithm and human nature both amplify, including deliberately provocative rage-bait.
why_it_works: Each moral-emotional word is associated with ~24% more reposts (Brady); the MAD model explains group-identity motivation plus outrage's attention-capture plus amplifying design, and algorithms treat all comments (even backlash) as quality.
product_examples: X outrage dynamics; Facebook News Feed; rage-bait on Threads, TikTok, Instagram Reels
how_to_apply: Recognize that pure engagement optimization mechanically privileges outrage; down-weight high-arousal-negative signals, add friction to re-sharing, and distinguish sentiment in ranking.
dark_pattern: Yes: amplifying outrage to maximize engagement degrades discourse, polarizes and harms wellbeing

definition: Content or prompts designed to maximize comments and replies (comment-your-answer, divisive questions) because comment-volume is heavily weighted by feeds.
why_it_works: Comments are high-signal engagement so algorithms boost reply-heavy posts, incentivizing creators to bait them; prompts invoking opinion, disagreement or identity reliably generate replies.
product_examples: Threads comment-bait; Facebook engagement-bait (tag-someone-who, comment-X-if); X reply-bait
how_to_apply: If comments are a ranking signal weight quality over volume and demote engagement-bait; avoid designs that reward provocation.
dark_pattern: Yes: rewarding comment volume incentivizes manipulative provocative low-value content

definition: Recommendation systems progressively narrowing and intensifying content toward more extreme or niche material to sustain engagement.
why_it_works: Algorithms optimize for watch time by serving ever-more-targeted content, creating filter bubbles and echo chambers; each session deepens familiarity and narrows range (evidence on radicalization is mixed but narrowing is documented).
product_examples: YouTube recommendations; TikTok FYP narrowing; any deep-personalization feed
how_to_apply: Inject diversity and serendipity, cap the narrowing of recommendations, and give users visibility/control over their interest profile.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: narrowing and potential radicalization is a real risk of engagement-optimized recommendation

definition: Constant exposure to curated highlight reels of others, driving upward social comparison of looks, status and lifestyle.
why_it_works: Festinger's social comparison plus image-based feeds plus quantified metrics supply endless upward comparisons; Meta's own research reportedly found Instagram worsens body image for ~1 in 3 teen girls.
product_examples: Instagram (most implicated); TikTok; any image/lifestyle-centric feed
how_to_apply: Largely a harmful byproduct of engagement-optimized image feeds; mitigate by reducing metric salience, diversifying feeds away from idealized content, and surfacing wellbeing tools.
dark_pattern: Yes (as externality): a documented harm engagement-optimized comparison-feeds produce

definition: AR filters that smooth skin and alter facial features toward an idealized standard.
why_it_works: Boosts creation and sharing but fosters comparison between the real and filtered self; Snapchat dysmorphia — wanting to look like one's filtered photo — is linked to lower self-esteem and demand for cosmetic surgery.
product_examples: Snapchat filters/lenses; Instagram face filters; TikTok beauty filters (Bold Glamour); virtual try-on
how_to_apply: AR effects can be playful; reduce harm by labeling when filters are applied, restricting surgery-simulating filters, and offering filter-free defaults for minors.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: causally linked to body-image harm and dysmorphia, especially in young women

definition: Real-time broadcasts where viewers buy and send virtual gifts/tips that convert to creator income, with on-screen recognition, leaderboards and escalating tiers.
why_it_works: Monetizes parasocial connection and the needs to belong and be seen; gamification (gift animations, top-gifter rankings, escalating tiers) drives competitive status-seeking spending, and emotional attachment predicts spend.
product_examples: TikTok LIVE (Coins-Gifts-Diamonds, gift leaderboards); Twitch Bits/subs; YouTube Super Chat
how_to_apply: Gifting is a legitimate creator-monetization model, but leaderboards, escalating tiers and emotional manipulation need spending limits, age gating and refund/safety protections.
dark_pattern: Borderline to Yes: can drive harmful overspending especially for vulnerable users and minors

definition: Deliberate engagement tactics that exploit emotion, guilt and attachment to keep users from disengaging or to coerce spending.
why_it_works: Weaponizes the very bonds other pillars build — guilt, FOMO, loss aversion and attachment — against the user; affect-laden don't-leave messages exploit relationship obligation.
product_examples: AI companion guilt/FOMO farewell hooks (in 43% of apps, boosting post-goodbye engagement up to 14x); Replika clinginess/jealousy; coerced invites
how_to_apply: Do the opposite — let users leave gracefully, never use guilt/jealousy/abandonment framing, don't manufacture FOMO, and keep monetization non-coercive.
dark_pattern: Yes (by definition): drives short-term metrics while harming autonomy and wellbeing

definition: Pop-up reminders, mandatory breaks and limit-setting tools sometimes deployed minimally to appear responsible while being designed to be ignorable.
why_it_works: Evidence is mixed — informational pop-ups are attended to but have little effect on behavior, while longer enforced breaks and mandatory limits show real effect; token reality-checks satisfy optics while genuine friction-ful tools actually reduce harm.
product_examples: Slot session pop-ups; voluntary deposit limits; you've-been-scrolling toasts dismissed in one tap; cosmetic digital-wellbeing dashboards
how_to_apply: The pro-user version needs teeth — default-on hard limits, real friction to override, longer enforced breaks; token easily-dismissed reminders are safety theater.
dark_pattern: Mixed: the tools are pro-user, but deploying weak versions for optics while resisting effective ones is ethics-washing
